svg.title: How the sign and size of a derivative decide a weight update
svg.desc: Three hand-drawn cards, each showing the same loss curve against a single weight w, with a tangent drawn at a different point. In the first the slope is positive two at w equals two, meaning raising w raises the loss, so the update rule subtracts and w falls to one point eight. In the second the slope is nought at w equals one, meaning w barely affects the loss there, so the rule leaves it where it is. In the third the slope is minus two at w equals nought, meaning raising w lowers the loss, so subtracting a negative pushes w up to nought point two. Each card spells out the arithmetic, w becomes w minus nought point one times the slope. A band notes that all three moves are the same line of code with a learning rate of nought point one, and that every one of them steps towards w equals one where the loss is lowest, without anything in the rule knowing that is where it is going.
svg.text: What a slope tells a weight to do
The same loss curve and the same update rule at three points. The sign decides the direction; the size decides the distance.
The rule subtracts, so w falls.
w barely affects the loss here.
The rule leaves it where it is.
Subtracting a negative pushes w up.
All three moves are the same line of code: w ← w − α · ∂L/∂w, with α = 0.1.
Every one of them steps towards w = 1, where the loss is lowest, without anything in the rule knowing that is where it is going.
